Haxe is a systems language.
We compile it like one.

Why build another
Haxe compiler?

Haxe already has the type system, the macros and the ergonomics. What it hasn't had is a compiler that goes straight to machine code, frees memory without a collector, and optimizes once for every backend. Rayzor does that, with the Haxe you already write.
We wanted native code, fast iteration, and control over memory while keeping Haxe's types and macros. Rayzor brings those pieces together in one compiler. These choices guide the implementation.
An optimization ships after it's proven correct. Drop insertion and inline are guarantees, not hints, so they run at every level, including -O0.
We verify optimizations before shipping them. Drop insertion and required inlining run at every level, including -O0, because program correctness depends on them.
The compiler works out when to free things. No pauses in the middle of a frame, and you can annotate one class at a time.
The compiler determines when to free memory, so there are no GC pauses during a frame. You can add ownership annotations one class at a time.
Same source, same binary
Deterministic codegen
MIR collections are ordered on purpose, so codegen is reproducible build after build.
MIR collections use a stable iteration order to keep code generation reproducible.
Don't redo work
Cache unchanged modules
Parsing, type checking, module caching and bundling all skip what hasn't changed. Caching is on by default.
Parsing, type checking, and bundling reuse cached work for unchanged modules. The cache is enabled by default.
Optimize once
Shared optimization passes
Every target is built from the same optimized program, so an improvement to one speeds up your native binary and your wasm module too.
Every target uses the same optimized MIR. Improvements to the shared passes carry through to both native binaries and WebAssembly.
Not a goal
Scope

Transpilation. The official Haxe compiler is very good at emitting JavaScript, Python and PHP. Rayzor has no such target and won't. Use the official compiler when you ship source, Rayzor when you ship machine code.

Benchmark results.

Same Haxe source on every target. Rayzor is faster than HashLink outright, faster than the JVM without paying its startup, and faster than hxcpp on floating-point work. Compile time is tens of milliseconds, not hundreds.

We run the same Haxe source on every target. Rayzor beats HashLink and the JVM, avoids JVM startup overhead, and outperforms hxcpp on floating-point workloads. Compilation takes tens of milliseconds, compared with hundreds on the other targets.
That compile column is the part you feel all day. No C++ toolchain to set up, no JVM to warm, no separate build step before you can run.
Short compile times make a difference when you run code throughout the day. Rayzor needs no C++ toolchain or JVM warm-up, and you can run source files directly.
starts executing while the optimizer is still working. And it's a cold number: the BLADE cache keeps every unchanged module compiled, so the second build compilation is instant.
starts executing while the optimizer runs. These are cold-build measurements. With the BLADE cache, unchanged modules are already compiled, so compilation on the second build is instant.

Work distribution is chunk-stealing rather than static bands: workers claim row ranges from a shared atomic cursor until the range is exhausted. Static bands lose the join to the slowest core, since an E-core band runs three to four times longer than a P-core band. Stealing self-balances heterogeneous cores without knowing the topology.

Workers claim chunks of rows from a shared atomic cursor until all rows are processed. With fixed row assignments, an E-core can take three to four times longer than a P-core, holding up the whole call. Chunk stealing lets faster cores take more work without needing to know the CPU topology.

architecture.html: Rayzor is a native code generator, not a source-to-source backend: every backend emits machine code, WASM bytecode, or C used as an assembler. What it adds over the official compiler is a tiered runtime and a single optimization pipeline shared by every backend — code starts executing immediately, and only what proves hot pays compilation cost.

Rayzor adds a tiered runtime and a shared optimization pipeline to Haxe. Backends emit machine code, WebAssembly, or C for native compilation. In tiered execution, code starts immediately in the interpreter; functions are compiled as they get hot.
Language transpilation is an explicit non-goal. There is no JavaScript target and none planned.
The supported output targets are native code and WebAssembly. There is no planned JavaScript target.

HIR still knows what the user wrote, so diagnostics and ownership analysis read naturally there. MIR is flat and typed, so one optimization pipeline serves every backend — that is the whole reason for the split. Type checking is not a separate phase; it is folded into AST lowering.

HIR preserves source-level structure for diagnostics and ownership analysis. MIR represents typed operations in basic blocks, which lets the backends share optimization passes. Type checking happens during AST lowering.

Ordering is load-bearing: inlining exposes Alloc+GEP for SRA, GlobalLoadCaching dedups metadata loads for BCE, BCE emits the invariant load LICM hoists, and LICM's clean loop bodies are what LoopUnrolling and LoopVectorization need.

Pass order matters. Inlining exposes Alloc+GEP for SRA. GlobalLoadCaching deduplicates metadata loads so BCE can remove bounds checks. BCE exposes invariant loads for LICM to hoist, preparing loops for unrolling and vectorization.
The interpreter is tier 0, the next three rungs are Cranelift, and Maximum is LLVM. Promotion compares tier ordinals, so a counter clearing several thresholds at once skips rungs.
Tier 0 is the interpreter, tiers 1–3 use Cranelift, and tier 4 uses LLVM. A function can skip tiers if its call count passes several thresholds at once.

is the safety-critical part. Function pointers cannot be swapped while JIT code is running, so a safepoint gates the swap: the promoter requests promotion, waits for the in-flight execution counter to drain to zero, swaps under a write lock, and returns to idle. Installs are monotonic — a pointer for a function already at a higher tier is dropped.

waits for active JIT calls to finish before replacing a function pointer. The promoter requests a safepoint, waits for the execution counter to reach zero, and swaps the pointer under a write lock. A completed compilation is discarded if the function has already reached a higher tier.
